To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic exposure of rat cortical neurons to low micromolecular concentrations of ATS (up to 10 μM), for 28 days, does not elicit neuronal death, oxidative stress or senescence.
long-term exposure to AMPH or MDMA promotes neuronal death and mitochondrial dysfunction in primary cortical cultures.
ATS chronic exposure to neurons promoted mitochondrial dysfunction and elicitation of neuronal death in a dose-dependent manner, which was not dependent on glutamate receptor activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chronic impact of low doses of ATS on neuronal cultures.
the chronic effects of ATS on the brain and the neuronal aging process.
the impact of ATS chronic exposure to neurons, a topic that has not been addressed before.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neuronal cultures exposed to low micromolars of ATS for 28 DIV are not senescent, but they are chronically exposed to a toxic environment that can promote neuronal death.
chronic exposure of neuronal cultures to ATS promotes mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress and neuronal death, and that AMPH is more toxic than MDMA.
the chronic use of ATS at concentrations equal or below 10μM, as well as the use of ATS by patients with psychiatric disorders, would be safe to neurons and brain health.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

chronic neuronal exposure to low micrormolar concentrations of AMPH or MDMA, similar to those found in the brains of chronic ATS abusers, does not promote accelerated neuronal senescence but rather neuronal dysfunction and death.
the chronic exposure to ATS at low concentrations (10 μM) does not promote oxidative stress or neuronal death in cortical neurons.
chronic exposure of neurons to low micromolars of ATS promotes a decrease in the number and size of both neuronal and astroglial cells, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chronic exposure to low concentrations of AMPH and MDMA, as low as 10 μM, is not toxic to primary rat neuronal cultures.

chronic exposure of neurons to low micromolars of ATS up to a period equal to 28 DIV does not promote neuronal senescence, but it does promote neuronal death and oxidative stress, which are not prevented by glutamatergic receptor antagonists.
low micromolar levels of ATS are not toxic to neurons.
